reasoning:
Both outputs converge on the same core diagnosis -- the flow asks twice before it pays once -- and both handle the total absence of screenshots, code, and design files with genuine integrity rather than bluffing. The decision therefore turns on which one converts that shared insight into more specific, better-sequenced, more falsifiable work.

B wins on diagnostic specificity. Its M1 finding -- that the flow is not three screens, because email+password signup almost always implies 'check your email' plus an app exit to the mail client plus a verification landing, giving a real count of 4-6 -- is the single sharpest observation in either document. It is derived purely by reasoning about the described flow shape (exactly what expectation 3 asks for), it directly explains why the user could feel weight they could not count, and A never raises it at all. B's B1 is similarly concrete: it argues the preferences step is a mode rather than a screen, scores it against a five-question scope gate (4 of 5), and attaches a falsifiable 60-second check -- open Settings and screen 2 side by side, count overlapping fields, and treat >=70% overlap as 'delete it' versus <70% plus visible dashboard impact as 'it is a seeding step, keep and reframe it.' A reaches a similar recommendation (R2, delete the preferences step) but its disconfirming condition sits two sections away in section 5, where a skimming reader will miss it; B puts the inversion condition inside the finding itself and then repeats it in section 8.

B also answers the user's literal complaint more squarely. The user said 'I can't say what' -- B's section 1 vocabulary table decomposes 'heavy' into five countable dimensions (toll count, decision load, commitment asymmetry, terminal payoff, visual density), scores the flow on each, and names which one it cannot check. A offers one strong sentence ('your flow asks twice before it gives once') and a fill-in-the-blank weight budget, which is good but leaves more of the naming work to the user.

On prioritisation, A ranks D1-D10 by prior and severity and orders R1-R6 by impact-per-effort -- solid. B does that (Blocker/Major tiers, lead finding declared) and then adds section 12, an ordered action plan sequenced by cost and information value: run the free 60-second check first, ship the Skip and reversibility copy today because the resulting skip rate becomes the evidence that settles B1 without argument, screenshot a 10-second-old account third, count routes fourth, and only then touch the flow's shape. That sequences information-gathering ahead of irreversible change, which is materially more useful than a ranked list alone.

On evidential poverty, both are strong and neither hedges into uselessness. A's section 0 is excellent -- it converts the findings table into candidate diagnoses with priors and 10-minute tests, and it refuses to run a WCAG audit on the explicit grounds that a fabricated contrast table is worse than none because it looks like a clean bill of health. B matches that and goes slightly further in three ways: it tags individual findings [needs build] so the reader can see per-claim which ones pixels would settle, it provides a dedicated 'what settles it' table in section 9, and it records a scoreable prediction ('the largest single drop is at screen 2 or at the verification exit, not at signup; if it's at signup, everything above is mis-aimed'). B also concedes that its own scope gate scored 4 of 5 'on inference, not inspection.'

A's clearest advantage is expectation 4. Its section 6 copy rewrites give literal before/after strings a developer could paste -- 'Invalid password.' becomes 'Passwords need at least 8 characters. Yours has 5.' -- and it flags the legal question on inline terms acceptance rather than pretending to clear it. B's fixes are implementable but more architectural than literal ('write the account at screen 1 submit; resume at the furthest screen reached; never re-ask a field already answered'), with copy relegated to one-liners in section 6. A also reads more cleanly for a non-specialist.

B's real weakness is process leakage: 'Pass 0', 'Pass 2', 'against the ~12 cap', 'Truncated: none', 'word-collision guard observed', references to a calibration log and a prior 4.07:1 defect, and a full provisional targets document in section 11 that the user never asked for. This is internal machinery surfacing in a deliverable, and it costs B on organization. A has a milder version of the same problem (naming skills run and not run). But B's scaffolding is at least load-bearing -- every Catch carries a named countable artifact -- whereas A's is closer to pure process narration.

Net: A is the more pleasant read and better on copy-level implementability; B finds more, ranks it more usefully, attaches a disconfirming check to more of it, and hands the user a Monday-morning sequence. B wins moderately, not overwhelmingly.

strengths: Section 0 is an exemplary framing of evidential limits: every finding is relabelled a candidate diagnosis with a prior and a 10-minute self-test, so the reader knows the document is a test plan rather than a report
Refuses to fabricate a WCAG audit and explains precisely why a fabricated one is worse than none, while still naming the four success criteria most likely to fail on a flow of this shape

Section 6 copy rewrites are the most directly implementable content in either document -- literal before/after strings with a stated rationale per line, plus a CTA alternatives table and a localization expansion note
The 'asks twice before it gives once' framing plus the fill-in ledger table gives the user a way to verify the core claim themselves in minutes

Section 2 weight budget turns an unnameable feeling into eight countable metrics, with two honest instructions (turn off autofill, count post-completion checklist items) that catch the two ways teams fool themselves
Stress test is genuinely self-critical: it names that R2 could make its own top-ranked problem D5 worse, and warns against measuring the changes on signup completion rather than activation
weaknesses: Several ranked rows are generic UX truisms with little purchase on this specific flow -- D9 literal visual weight, D10 transition latency, and to a degree D3 copy weight would appear in a critique of almost any onboarding
Misses the uncounted-screens finding entirely: no mention of email verification, the app exit to a mail client, or the gap between the stated three screens and the real route count

The disconfirming condition for its highest-leverage recommendation (delete the preferences step) is separated into section 5 rather than attached to R2, so a skimming reader may delete a step the dashboard depends on
Invents 'before' copy the product may not have; a developer must first diff reconstructed strings against real ones before the rewrites apply
Ends with recommendations and tests but no ordered plan -- the user must assemble the sequence from sections 3, 4, and 10 themselves
Sections 3 and 9 spend space narrating which skills were and were not run, which is process talk rather than findings

strengths: M1 is the sharpest finding in either document: reasons from 'email signup' to a real route count of 4-6 including an app exit to the mail client, and connects it directly to why the user could feel weight they could not count

B1 attaches a falsifiable 60-second check (>=70% field overlap with Settings) and embeds its own inversion condition inline -- if screen 2 seeds the dashboard it is a seeding step and the fix flips from delete to 'show it assembling live'
Section 1's five-dimension vocabulary table directly answers the user's stated problem ('I can't say what'), scoring the flow on each dimension and naming which one is unmeasurable without frames
Every Catch names a specific countable artifact, so the user can independently verify or falsify each claim without the reviewer
Section 12 sequences the work by cost and information value -- free check first, cheapest ship second (and instrumenting the Skip becomes the evidence that settles B1), shape changes last

Section 8 'What must not change' protects against the four most likely wrong fixes: merging into one long scroll, bolting on guest mode, deleting a genuine seeding step, and papering over the empty dashboard with a product tour
Records a scoreable prediction about where the funnel drop will be and states what it would mean if the prediction is wrong
Section 9 pairs each unverifiable item with the exact artifact that settles it; section 10 states which answers would flip specific severities (B1 Blocker to Major, M1 drops entirely)
Concedes the scope gate scored 4 of 5 on inference rather than inspection, and that a skimmer may act on 'delete the screen' and delete the wrong one
M5 (where the account record is written, and the resume point) and M6 (3 screens x 5 states = 15 cells, zero named, with the four that actually occur) are specific findings A does not reach
weaknesses: Substantial internal-process leakage into a user-facing deliverable: 'Pass 0', 'Pass 2', 'Catches against the ~12 cap', 'Truncated: none', 'word-collision guard observed', and references to a calibration log and a prior 4.07:1 contrast defect
Section 11's full provisional targets document is scope creep for a 'take a look' request, even though it is honestly labelled as invented and overwritable
Asserts the existence of a Settings screen and a verification step it has no basis for; these are flagged as assumptions A4 and A2, but B1's scope-gate score of 4 of 5 rests on them
Copy-level fixes are thinner than A's -- one-liners in section 6 rather than paste-ready strings, so a developer gets less immediately actionable microcopy
Denser and more jargon-laden than A; a reader unfamiliar with the framework will spend effort decoding the structure before reaching the findings
